Sensory Ganglia Sensory ganglia receive afferent impulses directed towards the CNS. Sensory ganglia are associated with cranial nerves ( cranial ganglia) and dorsal roots of spinal nerves ( aka spinal ganglia) . Neuronal cell bodies in sensory ganglia are large and accompanied by thin extensions of small glial satellite cells . Sensory ganglia have a distinct connective tissue capsule and an internal framework linked to the nerves’ connective tissue layers. Neurons in sensory ganglia are pseudounipolar , relaying information from the ganglion’s nerve endings to the spinal cord's gray matter via synapses with local neurons.

Autonomic Nerves and Ganglia Autonomic nerves regulate involuntary activities like smooth muscle activity, gland secretion, heart rate, and more, maintaining homeostasis . Autonomic ganglia are small, bulbous structures in autonomic nerves, typically containing multipolar neurons . Some autonomic ganglia are located within organs , notably in the digestive tract walls , forming intramural ganglia . The capsules of these ganglia may blend with local connective tissue , with a less distinct boundary. Neurons in autonomic ganglia are also enveloped by a layer of satellite cells .

Structure of Ganglia in the Peripheral Nervous System Ganglia are ovoid (egg shaped) structures in the PNS containing neuronal cell bodies and glial satellite cells . They are supported by delicate connective tissue and encased in a denser capsule . Each ganglion has at least one entering and one exiting nerve , serving as relay stations for nerve impulses. The function of a ganglion (sensory or autonomic) is determined by the direction of the nerve impulse .

Bronchi: Structure and Function Lymphatic and Immune Components Numerous lymphocytes are found within the lamina propria and among epithelial cells . Mucosa-Associated Lymphoid Tissue (MALT) MALT includes immune cells in the digestive, respiratory, and urogenital mucosae . It plays a key role in defending against pathogens that enter through mucosal surfaces. B lymphocytes in MALT proliferate in small spherical lymphoid nodules .

Larynx: Structure and Function Epiglottis The epiglottis is a flattened structure projecting from the upper rim of the larynx. It serves to prevent swallowed food or fluid from entering the larynx . The upper, or lingual, surface of the epiglottis has stratified squamous epithelium . This epithelium transitions to ciliated pseudostratified columnar (respiratory) epithelium at various points on its laryngeal surface. Mixed mucous and serous glands are located in the lamina propria beneath the epithelium.

Larynx: Vestibular Folds Located below the epiglottis and vestibule of the larynx. The upper pair of folds in the larynx, known as vestibular folds . They are immovable and partly covered with typical respiratory epithelium . Contain numerous seromucous glands and occasional lymphoid nodules .

Speed of Transport Fast Transport : Both anterograde and retrograde transports are relatively fast, moving at rates of 50-400 mm/day . Slow Anterograde Transport : Involves the movement of the axonal cytoskeleton at a rate of only a few millimeters per day , corresponding to the rate of axon growth.

Axonal Regeneration in Peripheral Nerves Peripheral nerves have a higher potential for regeneration compared to CNS nerves. If the neuronal cell bodies remain intact, damaged or severed PNS axons can regenerate . The distal portions of severed axons degenerate as they lose access to new proteins and organelles. Surrounding Schwann cells dedifferentiate, discard myelin sheaths, and proliferate within connective tissue. Macrophages clear cellular debris and secrete neurotrophins to promote axonal regeneration.

Bidirectional Transport in Axons Types of Axonal Transport Anterograde Transport : Moves organelles and macromolecules synthesized in the cell body. Uses kinesin proteins to transport materials along microtubules from the perikaryon (cell body) to synaptic terminals. Crucial for delivering necessary components to maintain axon and synapse function . Retrograde Transport : Carries certain materials in the opposite direction . Uses dynein proteins to transport substances along microtubules from the periphery to the cell body. Transports materials like those taken up by endocytosis , including viruses and toxins . Useful for studying neuronal pathways using markers like peroxidase .

Process of Axonal Regeneration Chromatolysis : The cell body (perikaryon) swells. Nissl substance (rough endoplasmic reticulum) diminishes. The nucleus moves to a peripheral position within the cell body. Degeneration and Regrowth : The proximal axon segment near the injury site degenerates slightly but then starts to regrow. New Nissl substance forms as debris is removed. Guidance by Schwann Cells : Newly formed Schwann cells align to guide regrowing axons. These cells produce factors that encourage axonal outgrowth. Restoration of Function : Motor axons reestablish synaptic connections with muscles, leading to restored function.

Motor Neuron Innervation and Muscle Control Motor neurons innervate muscle fibers by forming motor end plates (MEPs) . The extent of innervation varies depending on the muscle's function: Precise control , such as in the extraocular muscles for eye movements, involves single motor neurons innervating individual muscle fibers . Larger muscles with less precise movements have motor axons that branch extensively, innervating 100 or more muscle fibers .

Structural and Functional Classification of Neurons Structural Classification Challenges Difficulties in Classification : Due to the fine processes emerging from cell bodies being rarely visible in tissue sections , structural classification of neurons by microscopic inspection can be challenging. Functional Subdivision of Neurons Sensory Neurons (Afferent) : Receive stimuli from receptors throughout the body. Motor Neurons (Efferent) : Send impulses to effector organs like muscle fibers and glands. Somatic Motor Nerves : Under voluntary control, typically innervating skeletal muscle. Autonomic Motor Nerves : Control involuntary activities of glands , cardiac muscle, and most smooth muscle.

Spinal Cord Cross-Section Structure In cross sections of the spinal cord, white matter is located peripherally. Gray matter forms a deeper, H-shaped mass . Anterior horns of the gray matter contain cell bodies of large motor neurons . The axons of these neurons form the ventral roots of spinal nerves . Posterior horns contain interneurons receiving sensory fibers from neurons in the spinal (dorsal root) ganglia . The central part of the gray matter surrounds the central canal , linked with the brain's ventricles, lined by ependymal cells , and containing CSF (cerebrospinal fluid).

Sensory Ganglia Sensory ganglia receive afferent impulses directed towards the CNS. Sensory ganglia are associated with cranial nerves ( cranial ganglia) and dorsal roots of spinal nerves ( aka spinal ganglia) . Neuronal cell bodies in sensory ganglia are large and accompanied by thin extensions of small glial satellite cells . Sensory ganglia have a distinct connective tissue capsule and an internal framework linked to the nerves’ connective tissue layers. Neurons in sensory ganglia are pseudounipolar , relaying information from the ganglion’s nerve endings to the spinal cord's gray matter via synapses with local neurons.

Keratin and Keratinocytes Keratinocytes in the stratum basale feature cytoskeletal keratins , intermediate filaments about 10 nm in diameter . As cells differentiate and move upward, the amount and types of keratin filaments increase . In the superficial keratinocytes, keratin represents half the total protein .

Distribution and Structure of Melanocytes In the epidermis, there's typically one melanocyte for every five or six basal keratinocytes (600-1200/mm² of skin). Melanocytes have pale-staining, rounded cell bodies attached to the basal lamina by hemidesmosomes . Unlike other cells, they do not attach to neighboring keratinocytes. Each melanocyte extends long, irregular cytoplasmic extensions between cells of the basal and spinous layers, ending in invaginations of 5-10 keratinocytes.

Interaction with Keratinocytes Neighboring keratinocytes phagocytose the tips of these dendrites (melanocyte extensions), ingesting the melanosomes. Inside keratinocytes, melanosomes are transported towards the nucleus by dynein . The melanosomes form a supranuclear cap in keratinocytes, absorbing and scattering sunlight. This cap protects the DNA of living cells from the ionizing, mutagenic effects of UV radiation .

Keratinocytes in the Hair Bulb The keratinocytes of the hair bulb are akin to those in the basal and spinous layers of the epidermis. They divide rapidly in the matrix region around the dermal papilla . Following division , they undergo keratinization , melanin accumulation , and terminal differentiation .

Composition : Bile is composed of bile acids, bile salts, electrolytes, fatty acids, phospholipids, cholesterol, and bilirubin. Hepatocyte Functional Domains and Bile Secretion Sinusoidal (Basolateral) Domains Functions : Process nutrients and other blood components. Secrete plasma proteins. Apical Surfaces and Bile Canaliculi Role in Exocrine Secretion : The apical surfaces form bile canaliculi, crucial for bile secretion . Hepatocyte Adherence : Hepatocytes adhere firmly with desmosomes and junctional complexes .
